title: Why Exponentials Are Magic
question: Is there a curve whose slope is just a copy of itself?

blocks.text: Last time, the coffee's gap to room temperature shrank at a rate **proportional to the gap itself**. Big gap, fast shrinking. Small gap, slow shrinking. What kind of curve does that?
Chapter 3 already dropped a hint. Every little step **multiplied** the gap by the same number. So let's start with the simplest multiplying machine there is: doubling.
Take something that **doubles every second**. After 1 s you have 2. After 2 s, 2 × 2 = 4. After 3 s, 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. We write that as $2^t$: the little t up top counts how many times we multiply by 2.
Doubling every second, after {scrub|n} s you have {calc|chain}.

Drag the number of seconds **below zero**, or onto a **half second**. Zero seconds means no doubling yet, so $2^0 = 1$. One second back undoes a doubling: $2^{-1} = \tfrac12$. And half a second has to be a number that, used twice, makes one doubling: $\sqrt2 \approx 1.41$, because 1.41 × 1.41 ≈ 2.
So the exponent doesn't have to be a whole number. It's just "how much multiplying has happened", and that can be a bit, a lot, or even negative.
Here are those doublings as a ladder of bars. Split each step into halves, then quarters, then tiny slivers, and move the magnifier around:
Wherever I put the magnifier, the step rises by the **same share** of its own height. Tall bars rise a lot, short bars rise a little, but always the same share.

That's exactly the coffee's property: the change is proportional to how much there is. And look at the last readout. As the steps shrink, rise ÷ height per second closes in on a number, about 0.69 for doubling. Hold that thought.

The reason in one line: $b^{t+\Delta t} = b^{t} \cdot b^{\Delta t}$. Over any step Δt the curve multiplies itself by the same factor $b^{\Delta t}$, wherever it is. So it always rises by the same fraction of its height.
I've seen $e^t$ in textbooks. Isn't $e$ just some random number mathematicians like? 2.718-something, whatever.
Let's not argue about it. Let's build a growth rule and see what number falls out.

Here's the rule: **grow by 100% of what you have, per second**. The lazy way to follow it is one giant step: after 1 s you have 1 + 1 = 2. But that's June's giant-step trick from Chapter 3. For the whole second we used the growth rate from the **start**, even though the pile kept getting bigger.
So take smaller steps. Two steps of 50%: 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25. Four steps of 25%: 1.25 × 1.25 × 1.25 × 1.25 ≈ 2.44. Every step grows a pile that has already grown.
More steps, more growth! With infinitely many steps we'd get infinitely much. I'm going to be rich.

blocks.q: Keep splitting the second: a thousand steps, a million, as many as you like. What happens to the total after one second?

options.why: Each extra split does add a little, but the extra shrinks so fast that the total levels off. It never gets past 2.72.
Splitting really does help: 2.25 with two steps, 2.44 with four. Growth on top of growth adds up.

options.text: It levels off, a bit above 2.7
options.why: Right. The totals creep up towards 2.71828…, and no number of steps gets past it.

blocks.text: It stalls! A hundred steps, a thousand, and it never gets past 2.718. So much for my infinite fortune.
With {scrub|n} steps of {calc|pct}% each, one second of growth gives {calc|total}.
That ceiling is the number $e$. It's what the steps close in on when they get infinitely small:
Now flip the widget to **shrink**. With $\left(1 - \frac1n\right)^n$ it lands on $1/e \approx 0.368$: 36.8% left, so 63.2% of the way gone. That's the 63% from Chapter 3's time-constant ruler!
And one giant step of −100% wipes everything out. That's my frozen coffee again. Tiny steps fix it, every time.
Jacob Bernoulli ran into this number in 1683 while asking what happens when a bank adds interest more and more often.

Now let's hunt with a ruler. We want a curve whose slope, at every point, is a fixed multiple of its height. The ladder says every exponential $b^t$ should qualify: $2^t$, $3^t$ and friends. Put a tangent on each curve and divide its slope by its height.

Drag the cursor along any one curve and the **slope ÷ height** readout doesn't budge. Every exponential copies itself, scaled by a fixed number. For base 2 that number is about 0.693 (the number the ladder's shrinking steps were closing in on). For base 3 it's about 1.099.
And for exactly one base the scaling number is **1**, so the slope curve lies right on top of the curve itself. Which base is it?
It's 2.718 **again**! The same number the tiny steps gave us. Two completely different hunts, one number. Okay, I take it back: $e$ isn't random at all.
Of course it's the same. "Grow by 100% of what you have, per second, smoothly" *means* slope = height. It's one wish wearing two costumes.
The ruler said base 2 has slope ÷ height ≈ 0.693. That's no coincidence: 2 is what $e$ becomes after 0.693 seconds of growing, $2 = e^{0.693}$. So
Base {scrub|b} is $e$ raised to the power {calc|lnb}.

Every positive base is some power of $e$. That power has a name, the **natural logarithm** $\ln b$, and it is exactly the slope ÷ height the ruler measured. Bases below 1 get a negative power: they shrink.
Real systems don't all change at the same pace, so let's put a knob in the exponent: $e^{at}$. The number **a** stretches or squeezes time.

Now slope ÷ height is exactly **a**, everywhere on the curve. Positive a: it grows (and grows faster and faster). Negative a: it shrinks towards zero, like the coffee's gap. a = 0: it just sits there.
The knob and the base are two views of the same thing: $e^{at} = \left(e^{a}\right)^{t}$. Every second, the curve multiplies itself by $e^{a}$.
With a = {scrub|a} per second, every second multiplies the curve by {calc|ea}.

blocks.q: Take the slope of $e^{2t}$, and then take the slope **of that slope**. What do you get?

options.why: That's what happens for $e^{t}$ (a = 1). Here a = 2, and each slope multiplies by 2.
The first slope gives $2e^{2t}$. The slope of *that* multiplies by 2 again: $4e^{2t}$. Taking a slope just multiplies by a, every time.
A common algebra slip. The a comes down as a plain multiplier and t never appears in front.

blocks.text: Wait, that's huge. For exponentials, taking a slope (calculus) turns into **multiplying by a** (just algebra).
Put a sticky note on that. In Chapter 7 this idea grows up into a trick that turns calculus into algebra for *every* signal.

For a **linear change rule with fixed coefficients**, like our coffee rule, we can try an exponential: plug it in and see which value of a makes the rule true. Other kinds of rules may need other shapes.

The coffee rule was $\frac{dT}{dt} = -\frac{T - 20}{\tau}$ with τ = 10 min. Our guess is $T = 20 + 70\,e^{at}$ (70 is the starting gap). Tune a until the guess's slope agrees with what the rule demands.
The algebra agrees with the slider. The slope of the guess is $a \cdot 70e^{at}$. The rule wants $-70e^{at}/\tau$. The $70e^{at}$ appears on both sides and cancels:
And it lands exactly on the dots we built by hand in Chapter 3. Guess-an-exponential works. The equation that pins down a is called the **characteristic equation**.
Let's try it on something that **bounces**. A mass on a spring is basically our drone under P control: pulled back harder the further it is from the target.
The spring pulls back with force $-kx$. Force = mass × acceleration, and acceleration is the slope of the slope. So the rule is:
Guess $x = e^{at}$. The slope of the slope is $a^2 e^{at}$, so $m a^2 e^{at} = -k e^{at}$. Cancel $e^{at}$:
With k/m = 4, we need a number whose square is **−4**. Hunt for one:
Squares are never negative. The blue parabola never gets down to the green line. So there's **no** such a. Our trick fails: springs just can't be described with exponentials.
But the spring is right there, bouncing happily. It *has* a motion. Maybe it's not the spring that's wrong, maybe it's our idea of what counts as a number?
…Hmm. I'll admit I said "no number" a bit fast. Every number I *know about* squares to something positive.
Keep an eye on this. Was Theo right? (Spoiler: he wasn't.)

items: $b^t$ means "multiply by b, t times", and t can be anything: $2^0 = 1$, $2^{-1} = \tfrac12$, $2^{0.5} = \sqrt2$.
Growing 100% per second in ever tinier steps levels off at $e \approx 2.718$. Shrinking the same way leaves $1/e \approx 0.368$: the 63% ruler from Chapter 3.
Every exponential's slope is a copy of itself: slope ÷ height is constant.
$e \approx 2.718$ is the base where that ratio is exactly 1. With $e^{at}$ the ratio is a.
Taking a slope of $e^{at}$ just **multiplies by a**. Calculus becomes algebra.
**Guess an exponential**, plug it into the rule, and solve for a. For the coffee, a = −1/τ.
For a spring the guess demands $a^2 = -k/m$, and no ordinary number does that. Yet.

items.q: Grow by 100% per second in 1000 tiny steps. After one second you have about…

options.why: $(1 + 1/1000)^{1000} \approx 2.7169$. More steps creep closer to $e \approx 2.71828$, but never past it.
That's one giant step. Each tiny step grows a pile that has already grown, so you end up with more.
Each step adds only 0.1% of the pile, not a whole 1. The total stays below $e$.

items.q: Which curve has slope = −0.5 × height everywhere?

options.why: That's $e^{-0.5t}$: the negative ratio means it shrinks, and the shrinking slows down as it gets smaller.
A wiggle's slope isn't a fixed multiple of its height: at the peaks the height is biggest but the slope is zero.
Check the sign of $x'$: slopes of $e^{-3t}$ come with −3, so $3x' = -9e^{-3t}$.
That's just $x'$. You also need to add the $x''$ term.

items.q: A tank empties following $h' = -h/20$ (time in seconds). What are a and the time constant?

options.why: Guess $h = Ce^{at}$: $a = -1/20$, and τ = −1/a = 20 s, the time to drain 63%.
Upside down: the rule divides by 20, so it's slow (τ = 20 s), not super fast.
A positive a would make the water level *grow*. The minus sign in the rule means draining.

blocks.text: Honest bookkeeping: Theo's "no number squares to a negative" is a mistake. It's just one we can't see yet. Next chapter, he gets to be wrong in the best possible way.
The drone and the spring **wiggle**. Exponentials only grow or shrink. Unless… a number could square to a negative?

bases.title: Slope ÷ height for different bases
bases.statusE: Base e: slope ÷ height is exactly 1. The curve is its own slope!
bases.statusOther: Slope ÷ height is {r} everywhere on this curve. Constant, but not 1.
bases.aria: Graph of an exponential curve with a tangent line at the cursor, and optionally its slope curve.
bases.describe: Base {b}, at t = {t}, slope divided by height is {r}.
bases.help: Pick a base, then drag on the plot (or use the slider) to slide the tangent along the curve.

expA.title: Put a knob in the exponent
expA.grow: a > 0: it grows, faster and faster.
expA.shrink: a < 0: it shrinks towards zero, like the coffee's gap.
expA.flat: a = 0: it never changes. Slope zero, forever.
expA.aria: Graph of e to the a t, its slope curve, and a tangent line.
expA.describe: a = {a}. Slope divided by height is {r} everywhere.
expA.help: Drag on the plot to move the tangent. The faint dashed curve is your previous a.

guess.title: Tune the guess
guess.tooFast: The guess cools too fast: its slope is steeper than the rule allows. Make a closer to zero.
guess.tooSlow: The guess cools too slowly. Make a more negative.
guess.match: Perfect match! a = −0.1 per minute = −1/τ. The guess obeys the rule everywhere.
guess.aria: Coffee temperature: the hand-built solution of the cooling rule and an exponential guess whose rate a is set by the slider.

square.title: Hunting for a with a² = −4
square.status: a = {a} gives a² = {sq}. Still {gap} too big. Squares never go negative.
square.springCaption: Meanwhile, the real spring (k/m = 4, no damper) bounces happily:
square.springAria: A mass on a spring bouncing up and down.
square.aria: Parabola of a squared with a horizontal line at minus four that it never reaches.

ladder.title: The doubling ladder
ladder.status: Wherever you look, a step rises by {pct}% of its own height. Per second, that's {r}.
ladder.aria: Bar chart of 2 to the t, one bar per step, with the magnified step highlighted and its rise marked.
ladder.describe: Magnifier at t = {t} s, height {h}. Each step multiplies by {m}, rising {pct}% of its height.
ladder.help: Pick a step size, then drag on the chart (or use the slider) to move the magnifier.

compound.title: Grow 100% per second, in n steps
compound.n: Number of steps in one second
compound.growOne: One giant step: 1 becomes 2. For the whole second, it grew at its starting rate.
compound.grow: {n} steps: {v}. Still {gap} below e, and each extra split helps less.
compound.shrinkOne: One giant step of −100%: everything is gone. June's frozen coffee again!
compound.shrink: {n} steps: {v} left, so {pct}% of the way gone.
compound.aria: Growth over one second built from n equal steps, with a dashed line at e (or at 1 over e when shrinking).
compound.help: More steps means each one uses a more up-to-date rate. Switch the rule to shrinking to meet Chapter 3's 63%.
